L1@P0: THE ALGEBRAIC BOUNDARY OF SO(2)-ORBITOPES
L2@P0: RAINER SINN
L3@P0: Abstract. Let X ⊂ A
L4@P0: 2r
L5@P0: be a real curve embedded into an even-dimensional affine
L6@P0: space. In the main result of this paper, we characterise when the r-th secant variety to
L7@P0: X is an irreducible component of the algebraic boundary of the convex hull of the real
L8@P0: points X(R) of X. This fact is then applied to 4-dimensional SO(2)-orbitopes and to
L9@P0: the so called Barvinok-Novik orbitopes to study when they are basic closed as semialgebraic sets. In the case of 4-dimensional SO(2)-orbitopes, we find all irreducible
L10@P0: components of their algebraic boundary.
L11@P0: 1. Introduction
L12@P0: An orbitope is the convex hull of an orbit under a linear action of a compact real
L13@P0: algebraic group on a real vector space. It is a compact, convex, semi algebraic set. This
L14@P0: paper focuses on the algebraic boundary of SO(2)-orbitopes, i.e. the R-Zariski closure
L15@P0: of their boundary in the euclidean topology. The algebraic boundary is a central object in convex algebraic geometry. It is for example closely related to the notion of a
L16@P0: spectrahedron by a result of Helton and Vinnikov, see [HV07], section 3. The notion
L17@P0: of a spectrahedron is of interest in convex optimization, namely semi-definite programming, see e.g. the book by Boyd, El Ghaoui, Feron and Balakrishnan [BEGFB94] or the
L18@P0: article [VB96] by Vandenberghe and Boyd, which contains a survey of applications of
L19@P0: semi-definite programming.
L20@P0: It is also an important object when studying the question, which orbitopes are basic closed semi-algebraic sets, i.e. defined by finitely many simultaneous polynomial
L21@P0: inequalities. This question has already been asked by Sanyal, Sottile and Sturmfels in
L22@P0: their paper [SSS10], that initiated the study of orbitopes in their own right (in section
L23@P0: 2 of this paper, they propose ten questions on orbitopes; our question is number 4).
L24@P0: Again, the notion of being basic closed relates to spectrahedra, because spectrahedra
L25@P0: are always basic closed semi-algebraic sets. On the other hand, for a given basic closed
L26@P0: semi-algebraic set, Lasserre developped in [Las09] a semi-definite relaxation method
L27@P0: that was further investigated by Helton and Nie in [HN09] and [HN10]. Gouveia, Parrilo
L28@P0: and Thomas constructed semi-definite relaxations of real algebraic sets in [GPT10] and
L29@P0: [GT11]. Recently, Gouveia and Netzer further investigated exactness properties of these
L30@P0: two methods, see [GN].
L31@P0: In this paper, we will restrict our attention to the special case of orbitopes of the group
L32@P0: SO(2) of real orthogonal 2 × 2 matrices, which is probably the simplest non-discrete
L33@P0: case. Already in this case, the algebraic boundary is hard to describe. A first family
L34@P0: of examples was done by Sanyal et. al. in [SSS10]. The authors proved that an infinite
L35@P0: family of SO(2)-orbitopes called universal SO(2)-orbitopes are spectrahedra ([SSS10],
L36@P0: Theorem 5.2). Their spectrahedral representation gives a determinantal representation
L37@P0: of the irreducible polynomial defining the algebraic boundary of these convex sets.
L38@P0: 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary: 14P05, 52A99; Secondary: 90C22, 22E47, 14Q05.
L39@P0: Key words and phrases. convex hull, secant variety, basic closed semi-algebraic set.
L40@P0-1: 12 RAINER SINN
L41@P1: If the SO(2)-orbitope is not universal, then the algebraic boundary tends to be reducible. We will focus on the question whether or not the secant variety to the R-Zariski
L42@P1: closure of the orbit we started with is a component of the algebraic boundary. Our main
L43@P1: result is the following statement, which deals with convex hulls of real curves in general.
L44@P1: Theorem. Let X ⊂ A
L45@P1: 2r
L46@P1: be an irreducible curve and assume that the real points X(R)
L47@P1: of X are Zariski-dense in X. Let C be the convex hull of X(R) ⊂ R
L48@P1: 2r and suppose that
L49@P1: the interior of C is non-empty. Then the (r − 1)-th secant variety to X is an irreducible
L50@P1: component of the algebraic boundary of C if and only if the set of all r-tuples of real
L51@P1: points of X that span a face of C has dimension r.
L52@P1: For two different infinite families of SO(2)-orbitopes, namely 4-dimensional SO(2)-
L53@P1: orbitopes and the family of Barvinok-Novik orbitopes, we will apply this result to prove
L54@P1: that the appropriate secant varieties are components of their algebraic boundaries. For
L55@P1: 4-dimensional orbitopes, we use a complete description of their faces by Smilansky, see
L56@P1: [Smi85], to find all irreducible components of their algebraic boundary. In the case of
L57@P1: Barvinok-Novik orbitopes, a result of the work [BN08] will be essential. In both cases,
L58@P1: our results can be used to characterise, when these semi-algebraic sets are basic closed.
L59@P1: Namely, we will prove for Barvinok-Novik orbitopes that they are not basic closed.
L60@P1: For 4-dimensional SO(2)-orbitopes, we prove the following statement:
L61@P1: Theorem. Let C be a 4-dimensional SO(2)-orbitope. The following are equivalent:
L62@P1: (a) C is linearly isomorphic to the universal SO(2)-orbitope C2.
L63@P1: (b) C is a spectrahedron.
L64@P1: (c) C is a basic closed semi-algebraic set.
L65@P1: To show the basic ideas of the paper, we will informallly consider the example of the
L66@P1: 4-dimensional Barvinok-Novik orbitope B4 (all the statements will be proved in this
L67@P1: paper): It is by definition the convex hull of the symmetric trigonometric moment curve
L68@P1: {(cos(ϑ),sin(ϑ), cos(3ϑ),sin(3ϑ)): ϑ ∈ [0, 2π)}
L69@P1: The Zariski closure X of this trigonometric curve is an algebraic curve of degree 6 in
L70@P1: projective 4-space. The orbitope B4 is a simplicial and centrally symmetric convex
L71@P1: set. By a theorem of Barvinok and Novik ([BN08], Theorem 1.2; or alternatively, by
L72@P1: Smilansky’s result on faces of 4-dimensional SO(2)-orbitopes in [Smi85]), it is locally
L73@P1: neighbourly, i.e. the convex hull of sufficiently close points on the trigonometric moment
L74@P1: curve is a face of the orbitope. This allows us to explicitly compute the algebraic
L75@P1: boundary of B4; namely, it consists of two components, a quadratic hypersurface and
L76@P1: the secant variety to the curve X, which is a hypersurface of degree 8 in this case. We
L77@P1: will show that the secant component intersects the interior of the orbitope, which proves
L78@P1: that it cannot be basic closed. This is easier to see, if we slice the situation with the
L79@P1: 2-dimensional coordinate subspace W spanned by the second and the last vector of the
